transcript: Luisa Rodriguez: Today I’m speaking with  Spencer Greenberg. Spencer is the founder   and CEO of clearerthinking.org and coauthor  of the book The 12 Levers: The Complete   Psychological Toolkit For Improving Your Life  — which is actually being released today,   so congratulations, Spencer. Thanks for coming on. Spencer Greenberg: Thanks so much for having me. Luisa Rodriguez: So at 80,000 Hours, we ask  people to think deeply about some genuinely   very distressing things — pandemics,  AI, human extinction, factory farming. But taking these issues seriously is  very difficult for multiple reasons,   including for me personally. They’re hard  emotionally: we’re talking about suffering   and death on an enormous scale. They’re  also really hard to truly comprehend:   I think the human brain struggles  to actually fathom the things that   we at 80K think might be true — everyone on  Earth might die in the next decade or sooner,   humans and other sentient beings might suffer  extraordinarily at some point (or already).   Even in the best case, the world might transform,  maybe for the better, but beyond recognition in   the span of a few years — which, despite that  being a positive thing, I still find very scary. I think all of that makes thinking about   these issues emotionally fraught  and also epistemically fraught. And some of these issues are further  exacerbated when you decide to spend   your career trying to solve these problems. We have to grapple with the fact that we  might be able to help, and every moment we   spend playing board games or on vacation is time  that we don’t spend trying to reduce existential   risk or help animals that are suffering. There’s also just so much uncertainty about   these risks, so we might kind of simultaneously  believe our work has incredibly high stakes,   but also maybe we’re wrong about the whole  AI thing and we’re all wasting our careers.  Some of us have to decide whether to have kids in  the next few years, or delay or skip it entirely,   because maybe the next few years could be  the most important ones in our careers.  And we have to grapple with the fact that  we think AI, pandemics, factory farming,   and other issues are massive world problems,  when many of our friends and relatives don’t   understand why we think that or don’t  care enough to change their behaviour.  And working on these problems can also be a source  of incredible meaning, so there’s a big positive   too, which we’ll talk about. But I think we want  to give some airtime to the way that this is   costly — both to kind of normalise some of these  issues, to talk about some things that can help,   and then also just to be like, “Thank you  for working on these problems anyways.   We see that you’re doing that, and it’s  hard, and we would like to help how we can.” I guess to start,   do any of these things resonate with you?  Do you struggle with any of them personally? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah, they absolutely  resonate with me. And I think we should   acknowledge these are incredibly difficult  topics to work on psychologically. You know,   we have constantly changing things in the AI  space. I can absolutely relate to the fear that   this could go really badly on many different  levels — from more benign harms to very severe   harms, or even existential catastrophe.  Topics like animal welfare, the amount of   suffering involved is staggering, and even  thinking about it can be really disturbing.   So I absolutely relate to these things, and  also say, yeah, these are challenging topics. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. I’m glad that we’ll  get to draw on both some of that life wisdom and   then also a bunch of your learned expertise. You  have a lot of expertise on self-improvement and   trying to be a better, more flourishing person  in general. But neither of us, I would say,   are experts on the particular intersection of  mental health and existential risk — though   I think your book is super relevant,  even though it’s not tailored to it. But to get a better sense of what issues  come up for people working on x-risk,   we did a bit of research ourselves: I spoke  to a couple of therapists who mostly treat   patients working on existential risks, and  your team ran a survey for people working on   very important but neglected global problems  — so x-risks, factory farming, building the   EA [effective altruism] community — and then we’ve  got your book that also, again, is super relevant. To start, can you say a bit  about the survey you ran? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. We surveyed people  who work on these high-impact cause areas like   existential risk and, as you mentioned,   animal welfare and AI. We ended up getting  about 60 to 110 respondents, depending on   the question — because some were optional and  some people dropped out during the survey. The basic questions we were asking about are: Do you experience psychological  challenges in this work?  How big are those challenges? What are the nature of those challenges?  What kinds of things have you done that  you think might be helpful to yourself,   or that you think might help others?  And yeah, I think we have a lot of  really interesting results from that. Luisa Rodriguez: Can you say a  bit about the headline results? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. I’ll first note that  these tended to be younger people that responded,   typically aged about 25 to 45, and typically  working for less than 10 years in the field. What we found is that very few people  were suffering from what you might call   a clinical disorder or generalised anxiety  disorder or major depressive disorder,   but the majority of people do seem to find  this work psychologically challenging. So   usually it doesn’t get to the point  of full-blown depression or anxiety,   but it doesn’t mean it’s easy. In fact, not  only did most people say that they experience   at least somewhat difficult psychological  challenges around it, but many people have   even considered leaving or reducing their  work in it because of these challenges. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, that is kind of  surprising, especially the last part:   people have considered leaving their  work but aren’t currently reporting   depression and anxiety. Do you think  there could be some other explanation,   and people actually are experiencing some  depression and anxiety? Or do you think maybe   those two questionnaires aren’t really capturing  what makes this so hard for people? Or it’s   actually just not that hard, and people aren’t  depressed or anxious as a result of these topics? Spencer Greenberg: Well, generalised  anxiety disorder and major depressive   disorder reflect certain patterns in the mind  that can be really painful and difficult,   but they don’t reflect all that can  be really difficult psychologically.   I think what we’re seeing here is that  people are struggling psychologically;   they’re just not getting to the point  of having those particular disorders. When we ran the survey, we asked people which   of a variety of different psychological  challenges they face from a list. In fact,   the median number selected was six different  psychological challenges of doing this work.   Forty-five percent said they at least  considered cutting back or leaving,   and also 52% said that it at least moderately  hurts their effectiveness or productivity. So I think the answer is that people experience a   lot of psychological challenges; they just  usually aren’t these full-blown disorders. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. Were there any other  findings that felt particularly surprising to you? Spencer Greenberg: One was that the most common  challenges people said they faced — which are   not necessarily the most severe, but it’s still  interesting to look at — were difficulty switching   off or having boundaries around work: 68% of  people said they had trouble switching off   after work. I think that actually really is an  issue, because it elevates your stress level,   makes it difficult to relax. I think  that can actually, even if it doesn’t   get to a full-blown disorder, have pretty  negative consequences over the long run. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, yeah. What were  the next couple of most common things? Spencer Greenberg: Imposter syndrome was really  common, at 60%. For those of you that don’t know,   that’s when you kind of secretly harbour  the fear that you’re not good enough,   or that you’re there by some kind of mistake  and you know you shouldn’t really be there. And then we also have burnout: 59% said  they had some experience with burnout,   which can mean different things to different  people. It can be a loss of motivation, it can   just be feeling too stressed to function. So a  wide range of things can contribute to burnout. Fifty-six percent said they experience guilt,   and then 54% said they experience  anxiety or worry around their work. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, OK. Those just  feel like very high numbers to me.   We’ll talk about most of those  things, and a couple of others. Before we start getting into  some of the concrete issues,   can you say a bit more about the book? Kind of  what it covers and your process for writing it? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. So our  new book — and we would really   love for you to check it out if it sounds  interesting — is called The 12 Levers:   The Complete Psychological  Toolkit For Improving Your Life. The idea behind it is that my coauthor,  Jeremy Stevenson, and I studied over 100   of the most popular self-improvement books,  and over 20 of the most used therapies — so   cognitive behavioural therapy, but also  many others. What we were looking for is   them saying any kind of method or technique or  telling you to do something to change your life,   and we made a giant database of everything they  said — which is almost 500 different techniques. And then our question was: what are  all of the psychological strategies   for improving your life? What’s  the high-level meta pattern here?   And I was worried we’d have 50 different  high-level patterns, but actually,   to my surprise, we were able to boil it down  to just 12 high-level psychological strategies   for improving your life. And that’s where the  name of the book comes from, The 12 Levers. We also looked at the evidence for these different  levers. And the goal of the book is to teach you   about what each lever is, how you can use it  effectively, and give you specific concrete   steps to put it into action. Each lever has  multiple techniques around it, sometimes there   are even dozens, so we try to pick what we think  are the most useful techniques around each lever. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. Again, it’s  helpful for all sorts of issues you might have,   but I was kind of blown away when I was  preparing for this interview. It’s just   a very relevant toolkit for  this subset of issues too. Let’s talk about some of the specific issues  that come up for people working on x-risks.   Actually I kind of want to start  with a slightly different point,   which is that I actually had a high when  I first started getting really bought into   existential risks being real. I guess not  just x-risks, but there being very pressing   global problems that people weren’t tracking,  and that plausibly could get a lot better. I think it felt like I learned something  important and true about the world, and as   a result I got to have this big opportunity  to work on something high stakes that not   many people were taking seriously. It felt  exciting and it felt like an opportunity. And   I think the ideas are also just intrinsically  interesting, almost like a good sci-fi novel. So I think there’s something enjoyable about that,   which I feel kind of strange and awkward  about. But from the conversations I’ve   had with therapists who work with people  working on these issues, this is kind of   a common experience. Did you have anything  like this, or do you know people that did? Spencer Greenberg: I think  it’s actually really common,   because if you have new information that  makes you feel like you have special   knowledge that’s important to the fate of  the world, that’s an incredibly attractive   idea. And we can see that idea growing  in popularity in many different domains,   right? There’s nothing unique about these ideas in  that way; people are drawn to special knowledge. In addition, it can really give meaning to  life. Having the sense of, “There’s something   important and meaningful for me to work on,”  that can be really motivating. Furthermore,   it can make you feel connected  to a community if there’s other   people involved; you can feel connected to  that community through these shared ideas. So yeah, I think in a way  it can be really appealing,   while it could also be frightening if you  kind of grapple with the gravity of it all. Luisa Rodriguez: According to some of the  therapists I spoke to — and it seems like   the survey backs this up — after learning  about these ideas, starting to work on them,   maybe some people have a bit of a high, but then  people can start to experience a kind of chronic,   low-grade emergency state. So kind of  the threat system being perpetually on,   because you’re regularly aware that humanity is  under threat, or that factory farming is causing   enormous unimaginable suffering right now, and  we’re not really on track to solve these issues. I think this can come with kind of hypervigilance,  and compulsive monitoring of news sites and X,   and the sense that you can’t slow down or  stop working — because things are on fire,   and we don’t have that much time  before things get catastrophically bad. Do you personally experience anything like this? Spencer Greenberg: I, for my whole life, have had  the kind of mind that tends to look for things   that could go wrong. So I’m a kind of worrier  personality; that’s always something that I’ve   dealt with. And over the years I’ve improved  tremendously on this, and it’s much less of   a problem for me now than it was when I was  younger. You know, like on the weekends I’d   have trouble even relaxing or enjoying the weekend  because I’d stress myself out with my thoughts. So I feel like I’ve found a number of tools that  really help, but I do think that’s my fundamental   disposition. Like I don’t ever expect to have  a different brain that’s not a worrier brain,   but I do expect to have tools that make it  all kind of easier that I can continue to use. But I think, especially with topics like  this — where they feel so big and important,   where they feel like they’re changing,  where people feel morally responsible   to contribute — you’re going to find this at  especially high rates, not just among people   born with brains like me, but probably  among a lot of other types of brains too. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. Do you buy that this is  a bad thing? I ask because there are plenty of   things that I worry about in my day-to-day life  that I give more worry than I think they deserve.   But these problems are exceptionally big, and  probably deserve more worry than we give them.   If we were actually going to have worry that  was proportionate to the size of the issue,   how much anxiety is the right amount of anxiety? Spencer Greenberg: There’s a lot to unpack there.  And if you go to cognitive behavioural therapy,   let’s say for anxiety, an exercise sometimes that  you’ll engage in is one where you consider the   evidence. So they’ll be like, “You’re worried  about this thing. You’re worried about how   your friend didn’t text you back. What’s the  underlying thought there?” Maybe the underlying   thought is like, “Maybe my friend doesn’t like me  anymore.” And then they’ll be like, “OK, why don’t   you consider the evidence for and against?”  You’ll consider the evidence for and against,   and often people will feel better after that, and  it will help them have more realistic thinking. And there’s a temptation, I think, if  someone goes to a friend who doesn’t buy into   these [existential risk] ideas, or even goes to a  therapist who’s used to practicing that technique,   where they’ll be like, “Consider the  evidence.” And that’s actually really   unhelpful in this situation, because chances  are, if you’re listening to this podcast,   you’ve already thought a lot about  the evidence — and if someone’s like,   “Consider the evidence for and against this  problem that you think is a horrible problem   being really bad,” you’re like, “Yeah, I’ve  thought about the evidence, and I think it   actually is really bad.” So that’s not the  way to go in these kinds of situations, right? But I think it’s also important to ask the  question, what is hypervigilance, and what’s   the point of it? Effectively it’s a state that’s  preparing you to take drastic action. Like there’s   something dangerous that’s coming: you’ve  got to go, you’ve got to act. Unfortunately,   it’s really not a healthy state to be in  all the time. It’s not good for your body,   it’s not good for your mind. It can  literally mess up things like digestion,   because it actually affects your digestion  when you’re in a hypervigilant state. You know, I like to think about professional  athletes here. Do professional athletes want   to be stressing their bodies all the time?  If you’re training to be in the Olympics,   and all you care about is the  goal of winning the Olympics,   are you just stressing your body to the absolute  limit? The answer is absolutely no, because   that is not the performance-optimising move. The  performance-optimising move involves genuine rest;   it involves variation of things. You’re not always  working just on that one skill set. You’re going   to have off days. You’re going to have days  where you’re practicing other things or doing   cross training or whatever — and that’s even  if you just care about optimising for the goal. So I think we have to be realistic  about like, what is this state,   what is it doing for us? And what  kind of beings are we realistically? Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I think the “what kinds  of beings are we realistically?” feels really   important to me. Part of my brain thinks that  I can just not be a human. I don’t know what   gave me this idea. I think it is something about  this community really valuing self-improvement   and feeling like changing parts  about yourself is kind of possible. I think some people think people can’t change,  people can’t improve. Spending lots of time   around the kinds of people who think they  can make big improvements to the world,   I think you also spend time around the kinds  of people who think that they can better   themselves — and that includes things like, “I  can work harder; I can boost my productivity.” Spencer Greenberg: Well, I think  there are a few issues going on here. One is that people can have a sense that the way  they get social credit is by being the hardest   worker or the one who’s doing the most good or  whatever. If you’re in a community that values   that, that can become a kind of optimisation  metric — even to the point of it being unhealthy,   and even past the point of it actually really  being admired. It’s just sort of the sense that,   “I’ll be admired more if I push  this way.” And I think that can   be an unhealthy dynamic of competing over  who can grind themselves the hardest. I   don’t think that is the way anyone would  want the community to be. But sometimes,   maybe people can perceive that, and  that can have negative consequences. The other thing is that, even if your goal  were just to get the maximum performance,   you have to be realistic about what kind  of body you have and what kind of mind   you have — and grinding all the way is not  actually the way to get maximum performance.   It’s a naive version of trying to get  maximum performance. It’s like thinking   that the way that you win a race is by going  at maximum speed at every single moment. No,   that’s actually how you get injured or burn  out, right? That’s not the way you win the race. Luisa Rodriguez: One thing that especially  resonated with me was this idea that status   is part of the motivation. I think I have this  narrative that the reason I want to work harder   is purely because of impact, but I think if I  really reflect, you know, there is a part of me   that wants people to think I work hard just  because they’ll admire me more. And there’s   a part of me that wants my manager to think I  work hard because I want to be a good student. So why does this feel important? I think  it feels important because when I try to   interrogate why I find it so hard to rest,  I think the main motivation is impact. But I   think that the fact that actually these  other motivations are in there feels   important for me to notice — because really,  deep down, it isn’t all about impact. Yeah,   it feels like there’s something there.  I don’t know. What do you think? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. This goes back  to the question of what kind of beings   are we? I would argue that we’re  beings with many different drives. And some of them are very low level — like  generally people will avoid taking on extra   effort unless they have some reason to.  Literally they’ll walk in straight lines   instead of curved lines, right? They’ll  take the path of least resistance. Well,   why is that? I think we have some drive to reduce  energy expenditure. Of course, you can override   it. You could have a goal that overrides it. But  I think it’s worth noticing that that’s a drive. I actually think we have dozens of these  drives. We have a drive to be accepted by   our social community, probably because we would  literally die if we weren’t 50,000 years ago. I think we have all these overlapping drives,  and then we have this kind of reasoning,   more rational part of our minds that’s coming  up with principles to live by and ideas that we   want to follow and things we believe in, et  cetera — but that’s operating amidst all of   these drives. It doesn’t override all these  drives. And that actually can create a lot   of internal conflict when the drives and that  more rational part are not gelling that well. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I want to come  back to the internal conflict stuff.   I think a lot of what we’re going to  talk about today has to do with that. Before we do, I’m curious if there’s anything  you found helpful in recognising and accepting   that the type of person you are is a human with  limitations. I just want to be the kind of being   that can work as hard as my values make me  feel like I should. Have you done anything,   something like kind of dealing  with the grief of it or something? Spencer Greenberg: Well, I mean, it is a very  powerful idea, that we’re such limited beings,   and that no matter how hard we work to be  unlimited beings, we’re never going to get   there. All of these things are just ideals  that we strive for and we won’t come close. For example, I really care about trying to  be rational, and I regularly see how far   I am from that goal. And you could let  that kind of undercut your motivation,   being like, “Oh man, I’m so far from that,” or  you can turn that around and you can say, “Hey,   I can keep becoming a better version of myself  and move incrementally towards this more ideal   form.” And that can be exciting. I don’t think  it has to be demotivating. It can be motivating,   actually: being limited, but seeing  how you can progress and improve. But I would also say that failing to accept  your limitations can actually be disastrous   towards the goals that you care about. So the more  accurately you can see yourself — what you are,   what your limitations are — the better  you can be at all the things that you   care about. Denying them is actually a  strategy that’s going to undercut you. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, totally. I guess there are  a couple of threads there, and I want to put pins   in a few of them and stay on this idea of the  threat system always being on, and that being   a thing that can feel maybe truth tracking and  important — because in some ways it feels like   the world is genuinely on fire — but also not good  for you as a human being. Not good for your work,   if you assume something like… Actually, not just  assume: I believe that it is probably just bad for   your work if your threat system is always on and  you are constantly feeling chronically on fire. One common way that people end up entering  this threat system and staying in it   is tracking world events. So maybe there’s  the release of a new model that seems super   impressive, or a blog post or an interview  with someone talking about how AI timelines   are even shorter than they thought, or  bad news about policy, AI regulation   stuff. What approach seems most helpful to  you in handling these kinds of triggers? Spencer Greenberg: I’ll use a parallel because  I think it’s helpful: news consumption broadly.   Many people find news of the world stressful  because the news tends to focus on bad things,   and also there’s bad things happening in the  world. So they read an article on X and they’re   like, “Ahhh, things are falling apart!” And then a  friend posts on Facebook and they’re like, “Ahh!” So my strategy for helping deal with this  challenge is I subscribe to a service that   just gives one news story a day, and  that is my news. Basically the idea is:   if it’s not important enough to  be the top news story of the day,   it’s probably not important enough to  care about. And in fact, funnily enough,   many days that’s not even important enough for me  to want to read it, and you know, they’re picking   one news story a day. It’s kind of crazy to  think about, but so much of this is noise, right? And I find that helpful for me: staying on top  of the important things happening in the world,   but not getting sucked into it and not  wasting time, and you’re not getting   stressed out about things needlessly, but  still knowing kind of what’s happening. Now, let’s say you’re in the field of AI, and  things are moving so fast. It may be even more   difficult to deal with, just because there is  information you really want to stay on top of   and it is changing a lot. And there, I would  say the same kind of strategy can be useful:   being really aware of where am I getting my news,   what are the good news sources, what’s the  stuff that’s going to keep me up to date? And then trying to block out all the noise, right?  You don’t need to constantly scroll down and get   every single new post on X about AI, a bunch  of which are probably complete exaggerations   anyway or bad takes. You know, figure  out your trusted news sources and that’s   where you’re going to get your information.  That’s how you can stay on top of things,   and then you don’t need to just constantly  passively consume all this other information. Luisa Rodriguez: Why do you think  people are so inclined to doomscroll? Spencer Greenberg: Well, it’s a bit of an  irony, because often people go to social   media as a form of avoidance or as a form of  attempting to unwind, right? So they’re like,   “I don’t want to think about this thing.  I’m stuck on this thing. Let me open up   social media.” Or like, “I’ve just been  working hard, let me unwind.” And the   irony is that they end up often in this sort of  hypervigilant state when they’re on social media,   where it’s like not even necessarily  doing a good job of getting them to relax,   or maybe they’ve avoided this one thing and  now they’re stressed out about this other thing   they’re looking at. So it often doesn’t  serve the purpose that it’s intended to. This actually connects to an idea from our  book, The 12 Levers. In our beta testing,   we were having people read the book.  This idea is one of these ideas that   our beta testers just kept bringing  up, like this was an unlock for them. It’s this idea that we call “glad you did it”  activities. The idea is that often we do things   that are serving some need, or that we believe  are serving some need — like rest, relaxation,   et cetera — but when we actually really  get down to it, we could swap them with   a different activity that serves the  same need, but afterwards you’re like,   “I’m glad I did that.” You’re not  like, “That was a giant waste of time.” I think a mistake people often make  is that they try to swap out those   activities with things that don’t serve that  need. So you as a human have a need to rest,   but what you might be doing to rest is going  and scrolling social media — which, you know,   maybe it is a little bit restful, but maybe  it doesn’t even serve that person very well,   and then afterwards you’re probably like, “Why  did I do that? That was not a good use of time.” Well, what else is restful? What else shares that  same need? Maybe walking your dog or going for a   walk in nature or having a call with a friend  or whatever it is. And maybe it takes a little   bit more planning to make that happen; it’s  not quite as mindless — but if you could swap   it out with something that serves the same  need at least as well, hopefully better,   but where afterwards you’re like, “I’m glad I  did that; that was a good use of time,” it can   not only serve our needs better, but actually  make life more meaningful and fulfilling, and   I think be more restorative so you are more ready  when now you have to go take action in the future. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. I can imagine that’s  in contrast to what maybe I’d be tempted to do   if I had this problem of doomscrolling. I’m  actually not a doomscroller. I am a scroller,   but I’m not a doomscroller. I think I’d  be tempted to be like, “A virtuous thing   would be to work” or do something that’s a  good use of time according to unrealistic   values. It feels like a really key thing  about this is it’s meeting the rest need;   it’s not meeting the goal of “be a  more productive person all the time.” Spencer Greenberg: Exactly, exactly. And that’s  a mistake people constantly make. They’re trying   to swap one need for another, which often  doesn’t work. You need to do meaningful work,   that’s great, but you’re trying to replace  your need to rest, and it doesn’t satisfy   your need to rest. It’s a different thing. And  actually, you can kind of grind yourself to a   pulp and make it hard for you to function  if you’re never letting yourself actually   satisfy that rest need. Or if your “rest” is  not actually restful, like you’re actually   stressed out doing your rest because you’re  scrolling stressful AI news or whatever it is. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, that makes tonnes of  sense. One need that people are trying to get   met is rest. It feels like for some people there  probably is another. I’m kind of just guessing,   because this isn’t a problem I relate to as  much, but I wonder if there’s something like,   “This is a true thing about the world.  It’s scary. I need to look at it. I need   to know the true thing so that I can be able to  track it, and not be snuck up on or something.”   It’s like wanting to watch a danger  approach because it feels safer,   even though that’s triggering the threat  system. Does that sound plausible? Spencer Greenberg: Absolutely. When people feel  like there’s a frightening thing in the world,   they’ll often track it. You look at early days of  the COVID pandemic, people were absolutely glued   to any source of information, couldn’t talk about  anything else. And I think it is that vigilant   system of like, “This really scary thing is there.  We’ve all got to monitor it really closely.” And that goes back to some of what we were  talking about before: you need a system for   monitoring it. That is important if that’s your  field, if that’s what you’re focused on. But   once you have that in place, it actually can give  you permission to not monitor other times, right?   But if you don’t have a good system in place,  then you might always feel like “I might miss   something critical” or “I might need to monitor”  because you don’t trust that it will be monitored. It actually reminds me of this idea of the Getting  Things Done productivity system, where oftentimes   when people have never done complex work before,  they have very ad hoc systems for keeping track   of things, so they never really are sure that  they’re on top of what needs to be on top of,   or that all their to-dos are there. And one  of the insights of Getting Things Done is:   have a single trusted system. Anytime you have  something to do, it goes in the trusted system,   so you know you will never miss it. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. So for the  husband and wife, it’s something like,   actually they’re seeing these disagreements  in some way that feels very hurtful or   personal attack-y or something. Oftentimes interpersonal  disagreements like that that are recurring are not   about the thing that they seem to be about.  There’s a deeper thing that they’re about,   like maybe it’s, “I just don’t feel like  you really love me. OK, last question: which  lever do you find that you’ve had to kind of keep   relearning? So you find it really helpful,  but it’s just really hard to make it stick,   maybe because the kinds of problems it helps  with are the kinds that you struggle with most. Spencer Greenberg: Lever 8 is about how to be  more productive. And we call that “tuning the   productivity equation.” There’s actually  a mathematical equation we came up with;   it’s actually literal. It’s about how much value  you produce, and it splits into three factors: The time you put in: the more  time you put into something,   all else equal, you’re going to  produce more of what you value  The efficiency: how much  [output] do you produce per hour  The importance of the thing you’re working  on: if it’s not important to you at all,   according to what you value, you get  no output in terms of what you value.  And I think that very often people who want to be  productive throw hours at the problems — because   in a way, it’s the simplest and most obvious.  And it does improve your productivity, as long   as you can keep the other things equal. But in  many cases — unless you’re underworking, that’s   one thing — but for many productive people, it’s  actually the worst way to get more productivity. And I think I’m prone to throwing more  hours at things, so that’s one that I   have to keep coming back to and be like, that  is not the best way to be more productive,   and remind myself of it. So it’s  an ongoing piece of work for me. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I feel like we could have  spent a bunch of time talking about that one,   and it’ll be interesting to a  lot of people listening. So yeah,   I encourage people to pick up the book.  It is available today. My guest today   has been Spencer Greenberg. Thank  you so much for coming on, Spencer. Luisa Rodriguez: Can you say a  bit about the headline results?

Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, OK. Those just  feel like very high numbers to me.

Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. Again, it’s  helpful for all sorts of issues you might have,

Luisa Rodriguez: According to some of the  therapists I spoke to — and it seems like

Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I think the “what kinds  of beings are we realistically?” feels really

Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I want to come  back to the internal conflict stuff.

Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, totally. I guess there are  a couple of threads there, and I want to put pins

Spencer Greenberg: I’ll use a parallel because  I think it’s helpful: news consumption broadly.

if it’s not important enough to  be the top news story of the day,
it’s probably not important enough to  care about. And in fact, funnily enough,
many days that’s not even important enough for me  to want to read it, and you know, they’re picking
one news story a day. It’s kind of crazy to  think about, but so much of this is noise, right?
And I find that helpful for me: staying on top  of the important things happening in the world,
but not getting sucked into it and not  wasting time, and you’re not getting
stressed out about things needlessly, but  still knowing kind of what’s happening.
Now, let’s say you’re in the field of AI, and  things are moving so fast. It may be even more
difficult to deal with, just because there is  information you really want to stay on top of
and it is changing a lot. And there, I would  say the same kind of strategy can be useful:
being really aware of where am I getting my news,
what are the good news sources, what’s the  stuff that’s going to keep me up to date?
And then trying to block out all the noise, right?  You don’t need to constantly scroll down and get
every single new post on X about AI, a bunch  of which are probably complete exaggerations
anyway or bad takes. You know, figure  out your trusted news sources and that’s
where you’re going to get your information.  That’s how you can stay on top of things,
and then you don’t need to just constantly  passively consume all this other information.
Luisa Rodriguez: Why do you think  people are so inclined to doomscroll?
Spencer Greenberg: Well, it’s a bit of an  irony, because often people go to social
media as a form of avoidance or as a form of  attempting to unwind, right? So they’re like,
“I don’t want to think about this thing.  I’m stuck on this thing. Let me open up
social media.” Or like, “I’ve just been  working hard, let me unwind.” And the
irony is that they end up often in this sort of  hypervigilant state when they’re on social media,
where it’s like not even necessarily  doing a good job of getting them to relax,
or maybe they’ve avoided this one thing and  now they’re stressed out about this other thing
they’re looking at. So it often doesn’t  serve the purpose that it’s intended to.
This actually connects to an idea from our  book, The 12 Levers. In our beta testing,
we were having people read the book.  This idea is one of these ideas that
